principles.text: Pick products with lots of searches and keyword difficulty under 10-20, so ranking on Google replaces marketing.
Marketing separates successful indie hackers from unsuccessful ones. Don't just build, sell it.
Validate an idea with a one-time payment; add subscriptions once you know what customers want.
Ship fast and in public. Your first startups will miss, so get them out of the way quickly.
Build a feature once three customers ask for it, and ask why they want it before building.

sampleQA.question: How do I pick my first product idea?

answer.text: Keep typing keywords you're interested in into Ahrefs until you find a cluster with keyword difficulty under 10, then build a product around them.
With difficulty under 10-20 and one or two backlinks, he says you're all but guaranteed the front page, so you never have to do marketing.
Don't try to create a market: if no one searches for it on Google, you have to create the demand yourself.
Choose a painkiller, not a vitamin. A vitamin may be fun to build but is much harder to sell.

sampleQA.question: Should I charge a subscription or a one-time fee?

answer.text: If you want to validate an idea, make it a one-time payment.
One-off B2C purchases mean little support and no feature treadmill, because customers don't pay monthly.
If you charge under $9/month, test a one-time payment on new users; he expects conversion rate and lifetime value to go up.
Don't sell lifetime deals if your startup has recurring per-user costs.

sampleQA.question: My AI product is basically a wrapper. How do I compete?

answer.text: When everyone uses the same models, you differentiate on marketing and a good interface.
Build a moat by stacking models: HeadshotPro runs about 15 AI models in one pipeline, unlike ProfilePicture.AI, which had no moat.
Don't build on hype. Use SEO and backlinks so the product lasts after the attention fades.
Pick boring niches usually done by humans and automate them; nobody else wants to build there.
